# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XVI. TIT FOR TAT

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

With Grace, coming to a decision meant taking immediate action. She wasted no time in executing her plan. Following her return from school the following day, she departed the manse and went down the Glen. Edmund Carrow fell in with her when she went by the post office.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0000 }

“Mother sent me on an errand to Mrs. Kerr’s house,” he said. “Grace, where are you heading?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0001 }

“I am going somewhere on church business,” Grace stated haughtily. Because she offered no extra details, Edmund felt somewhat rejected. A short period of quiet followed as they continued walking. Warmth and wind filled the night, which possessed a pleasant, piney fragrance. Gray, gentle, and lovely waters lay past the sand dunes. Carrying a cargo of crimson and gold leaves, the Glen stream resembled magical boats. Within the buckwheat stubble-land belonging to Mr. James Coyle, which displayed lovely shades of brown and red, a crow parliament convened to conduct serious discussions concerning the well-being of crowland. Grace heartlessly disrupted the grand gathering when she scaled the fence and launched a fractured rail toward it. Right away, noisy caws and beating dark wings crowded the atmosphere.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0002 }

“What made you do that?” Edmund asked accusingly. “They were enjoying themselves so much.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0003 }

“Oh, I detest crows,” Grace remarked breezily. “They have such dark feathers and sneaky ways that I am certain they are deceitful. You see, they rob the eggs of small birds right from their nests. I witnessed a crow doing that very thing on our lawn during the previous spring. Edmund, why is your face so pale today? Were you suffering from that toothache once more during the night?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0004 }

A shudder ran through Edmund.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0005 }

“Indeed—it was terrible. Sleep was completely impossible for me—consequently, I simply walked back and forth across the room and pictured myself as a martyr from the early Christian era undergoing torment on Nero’s orders. For a period, that provided a great deal of relief—and after that, my condition deteriorated to the point where my imagination failed me entirely.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0006 }

“Were you crying?” Grace asked with concern.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0007 }

“No—yet I stretched out on the floor and groaned,” Edmund admitted. “Thereupon the girls entered, and Bess placed cayenne pepper inside it—which aggravated it—Izzy forced me to keep a gulp of cold water inside my mouth—and I was unable to endure it, so they summoned Tabitha. Tabitha stated that it served me right because I sat up in the chilly garret yesterday composing poetry trash. However, she kindled the kitchen fire and fetched me a hot-water bottle, which halted the toothache. The moment I felt improved, I informed Tabitha that my poetry was not trash and that she was no judge. Then she remarked no, thank goodness she was not, and she possessed no knowledge concerning poetry other than it was largely a heap of lies. Now you are aware, Grace, that is not true. That represents one reason I enjoy composing poetry—you are able to state so many matters within it that are true within poetry but would not be true within prose. I informed Tabitha as much, yet she instructed me to cease my jawing and get to sleep before the water cooled down, or she would abandon me to discover whether rhyming would heal a toothache, and she trusted it would prove to be a lesson to me.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0008 }

“Why do you not head over to Kettlebridge to see the dentist and have that tooth removed?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0009 }

Edmund shivered again.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0010 }

“They wish for me to—yet I am unable to. The pain would be immense.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0011 }

“Does a bit of hurt frighten you?” Grace inquired scornfully.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0012 }

Edmund flushed.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0013 }

“Being injured is something I despise, and it would cause great suffering. My decision to depart must be made by me first, as Father mentioned he would not force my leaving until then.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0014 }

“The pain would not endure for as great a duration as the toothache,” Grace contended, “Five bouts of toothache have afflicted you. Should you simply attend an appointment to possess it extracted, subsequent unpleasant nights would cease. A tooth was extracted from me on one occasion. My cries lasted for a brief instant, yet everything concluded thereafter—save for the hemorrhaging.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0015 }

“What’s most terrible is the bleeding—it is so hideous,” Edmund exclaimed. “Last summer, when Kit sliced his foot, it simply nauseated me. Tabitha mentioned that I appeared closer to passing out than Kit himself. Yet seeing Kit injured was something I could not endure, either. People are constantly being injured, Grace—and it is terrible. Seeing anything in pain is simply unbearable for me. It creates an urge in me to just run—and run—and run—until they are beyond my hearing or sight.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0016 }

“It is pointlessly dramatic to make a scene when someone suffers an injury,” Grace remarked, shaking her ringlets. “Naturally, you must cry out if your injury is severe—plus blood causes a mess—and I also dislike watching others suffer. However, running away holds no appeal for me—my wish is to proceed to work and assist them. On many occasions, your father must inflict pain on people so as to heal them. If he fled, what would become of them?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0017 }

“I never stated that I was going to run; I merely expressed a desire to do so, which is not the same. Assisting others is also something I wish to do. However, I truly desire a world free from hideous and terrible realities, where all things are instead joyful and lovely.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0018 }

“Well, let us not ponder things that do not exist,” Grace remarked. “When all is said and done, existing offers plenty of enjoyment. Being dead would mean no toothache for you, yet wouldn’t being alive be far preferable to being dead? For my part, I would choose it a hundredfold. Oh, Dan Coyle is approaching. His trip down to the harbour was to get fish.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0019 }

“I detest Dan Coyle,” Edmund stated.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0020 }

“I feel the same way. Every one of us girls does. I intend to just stroll by without giving him any attention whatsoever. Keep your eyes on me!”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0021 }

Grace therefore strutted by Dan, her chin thrust forward and her face wearing a disdainful look that deeply wounded his spirit. Turning around, he yelled toward her retreating back.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0022 }

“Pig-girl! Pig-girl!! Pig-girl!!!” with a growing intensity of offense.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0023 }

Grace continued forward, appearing unaware. Nevertheless, her lip shook just a bit from a feeling of indignation. She recognized that she could not compete with Dan Coyle in swapping insults. She desired that Kit Carrow had accompanied her rather than Edmund. Had Dan Coyle ventured to term her a pig-girl while Kit was listening, Kit would have knocked him into the dust. Yet Grace never thought to look to Edmund for that, or hold it against him for failing to do so. Edmund, as she was aware, did not engage in fights with other boys. Wilfred Clow from the north road was the same. The odd thing was, whereas she looked down on Wilfred as a coward, she never thought to look down on Edmund. It was merely that he appeared to her as a resident of his very own realm, where other customs ruled. Grace would just as readily have anticipated a starry-eyed young angel to beat up filthy, freckled Dan Coyle on her behalf as Edmund Carrow. She would have held nothing against the angel and she held nothing against Edmund Carrow. Yet she longed for robust Kit or Tobias to have been present and Dan’s affront kept stinging her spirit.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0024 }

The paleness had left Edmund's face. A deep crimson flush covered him, and shame and fury dimmed his lovely eyes. That he should have taken revenge for Grace was clear to him. Kit would have jumped straight into the fray and forced Dan to swallow his statements with bitter seasoning. Ritchie Warren would have flooded Dan with even nastier "names" than those Dan had used against Grace. Yet Edmund was incapable—utterly incapable—of "calling names." He was certain that he would be defeated. The crude, lewd taunts that Dan Coyle wielded in endless supply were things he could neither imagine nor speak. Furthermore, regarding a combat with fists, Edmund had no ability to fight. The thought of it repelled him. It was violent and sore—and, most terrible of all, it was hideous. Kit’s joy in a periodic brawl remained totally incomprehensible to him. Even so, he longed to be able to beat Dan Coyle. Extreme humiliation consumed him because Grace Ashdown had suffered an insult while he stood by, and he had made no effort to avenge her. It seemed certain to him that she held him in contempt. She had refrained from addressing a single word to him after Dan had labeled her pig-girl. When the point arrived where their paths split, he experienced relief.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0025 }

Grace also felt relief, but her reasons were not the same. Her desire for solitude stemmed from a sudden wave of apprehension regarding her mission. The initial spark had faded, particularly after Dan damaged her pride. Although she was bound to complete the task, her driving passion had vanished. Her purpose was to visit Lionel Fairlie and request his return to church, yet she was starting to dread him. The undertaking that appeared so straightforward and uncomplicated back at the Glen appeared quite otherwise in this location. Rumors about Lionel Fairlie had reached her ears, and she was aware that even the oldest students at school feared him. What if he insulted her with a cruel name—she understood he was prone to such behavior. Insults were unbearable to Grace—they broke her spirit much faster than a physical hit. Nevertheless, she was determined to proceed—Grace Ashdown never backed down. Failing to do so might force her father to depart from the Glen.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0026 }

Reaching the conclusion of the lengthy lane, Grace arrived at the dwelling—a spacious, ancient-style residence flanked by a line of disciplined Lombardies. Lionel Fairlie sat in person upon the rear veranda, engaged in reading a newspaper. His large canine companion remained by his side. From the rear, within the kitchen, a noisy rattling of tableware echoed from where his housekeeper, Mrs. Wilson, prepared the evening meal—a furious rattling, because Lionel Fairlie had recently engaged in a dispute with Mrs. Wilson, leaving each of them in a dreadful mood as a result. As a consequence, the moment Grace walked onto the veranda and Lionel Fairlie dropped his newspaper, she encountered the fiery gaze of a deeply annoyed individual.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0027 }

In his own manner, Lionel Fairlie was a somewhat handsome figure. Across his wide chest cascaded a long red beard, and his large head bore a thick mane of red hair that remained untouched by grey despite his age. No wrinkles marked his tall, pale forehead, and the intensity of his stormy youth could still ignite his blue eyes. Depending on his whim, he possessed the capacity to be exceedingly charming or exceptionally frightening. Intent with such worry on fixing the circumstance concerning the church, poor Grace had encountered him during one of these frightening states.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0028 }

Because he was unaware of her identity, his look toward her was one of dislike. Girls possessing laughter, fire, and high spirits were what Lionel Fairlie preferred. Grace appeared extremely pale right now. Colour was vital to the kind of appearance she possessed. Without the red in her cheeks, she came across as humble and downright ordinary. Her demeanor was fearful and full of regret, which aroused the aggressive nature within Lionel Fairlie’s heart.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0029 }

“Who on earth are you? And what brings you here?” he asked with a fierce frown, speaking in his deep, echoing voice.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0030 }

Grace lacked any response, a rare moment in her life. Never had she imagined that Lionel Fairlie possessed such a nature. Horror of him left her completely immobilized. Noticing her reaction, he became even more intense.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0031 }

“What is wrong with you?” he bellowed. “Your expression suggests you wish to speak but are afraid to do so. What is bothering you? Dammit, can you not speak out?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0032 }

Negative. Grace was unable to utter a sound. She could produce no speech. Her lips, however, started to shake.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0033 }

“In heaven’s name, stop weeping,” Lionel yelled. “Sniffling is something I cannot tolerate. Speak up and finish it if you have something to tell me. Holy Kitty, does a mute demon hold this girl? Stop staring at me in that manner—I am a man—there is no tail on me! Who might you be—I demand to know, who are you?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0034 }

The sound of Lionel’s voice was loud enough to reach the harbour. All activity within the kitchen came to a halt. Listening intently, Mrs. Wilson kept her eyes and ears wide open. Placing his massive, tan hands upon his knees, Lionel bent ahead and fixed his gaze on the pale, cowering face of Grace. To her, he appeared to tower above like a wicked giant from a storybook. It seemed to her that he was about to consume her entirely, flesh and bones included.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0035 }

“Grace—Ashdown—am—I,” she stated, speaking barely above a whisper.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0036 }

“Ashdown, is it? One of the parson’s kids, is it? I’ve heard about you—I’ve heard about you! Pig-riding and Sabbath-breaking! A fine crowd! What are you after here, is it? What are you after from the old pagan, is it? I do not request favours from parsons—and I do not grant any. What are you after, I ask?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0037 }

Grace desired to be a thousand miles from that place. Hesitantly, she uttered her idea in all its plain directness.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0038 }

“My purpose in coming—was to request that you—attend church—and contribute—toward the wage.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0039 }

Lionel stared angrily at her. After that, he erupted once more.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0040 }

“You insolent baggage—you! Who instigated you to do this, jade? Who instigated you to do this?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0041 }

“No one,” answered unhappy Grace.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0042 }

“That is untruthful. Do not utter falsehoods to me! Who directed you to this place? It was not your father—he lacks the courage of a flea—yet he would not dispatch you to perform what he dared not attempt on his own. I presume it was certain of those dratted elderly spinsters at the Glen, was it not—was it, eh?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0043 }

“No—I—I merely arrived on my own.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0044 }

“Have you pegged me as an idiot?” yelled Lionel.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0045 }

“No—it was my belief that you were a gentleman,” Grace whispered softly, and she truly had no intention of sounding sarcastic.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0046 }

Lionel sprang upward.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0047 }

“Attend to your own affairs. Not a single additional word from you do I wish to listen to. Were you not so young, a lesson would be taught to you about meddling where you have no business. Only when I desire clergymen or doctors shall I summon them. Until that time comes, I shall have nothing to do with them. Is that clear to you? Go away now, pale-face.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0048 }

Grace exited. Blindly, she stumbled down the steps, went out of the yard gate, and entered the lane. Midway up the lane, the daze of fear that gripped her passed away, and a reaction of tingling anger took possession of her. When she reached the end of the lane, she was in a temper so furious that she had never experienced its like before. The insults of Lionel Fairlie burned in her soul, lighting a scorching flame. Go home! She would not! Straight back she would go to tell that old ogre precisely what she thought of him—she would show him—oh, wouldn’t she! Indeed, Cheese-face!
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0049 }

Without hesitation, she turned around and trod back. Nobody was on the veranda, and the kitchen door was closed. Without a knock, Grace opened the door and entered. Lionel Fairlie had only just taken his seat at the supper table, yet his newspaper remained in his grip. Grace walked unyieldingly across the space, snatched the paper out of his hand, tossed it onto the floor, and stepped heavily upon it. After that, she turned to face him, her eyes blazing and her cheeks flushed red. She was so stunning a young fury that Lionel Fairlie scarcely knew who she was.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0050 }

“Why have you returned?” he barked, though his tone reflected confusion rather than anger.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0051 }

Without flinching, she stared back into those furious eyes that so few individuals were able to withstand.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0052 }

“I have returned to inform you precisely of my opinion regarding you,” Grace declared in distinct, resounding tones. “You do not frighten me. You are an ill-mannered, unfair, oppressive, unpleasant old man. Tabitha claims you are certain to end up in hell, and I felt pity for you, but that is no longer the case. A decade passed without your wife receiving a new hat—it is no surprise that she passed away. From now on, I intend to pull faces at you every time you are in my sight. Whenever I am positioned behind you, you will be aware of what I am doing. In his study, Father possesses a book containing an illustration of the devil, and my plan is to return home to scribble your name beneath it. You are an ancient vampire, and my wish is that you catch the Scotch fiddle!”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0053 }

Grace was as ignorant of the definition of a vampire as she was of the meaning of the Scotch fiddle. Having heard Tabitha utter these terms, she inferred through her tone that each was a terrible matter. Lionel Fairlie, however, was acquainted with the meaning of at least the second phrase. He had given Grace’s outburst his undivided, silent attention. As she brought her foot down with a stamp and stopped to catch her breath, he abruptly erupted into boisterous laughter. Striking his knee forcefully with his hand, he cried out,
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0054 }

“I swear you possess grit, despite everything—grit appeals to me. Here, take a seat—take a seat!”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0055 }

“I will not.” The fire in Grace’s eyes blazed with greater fury. It seemed to her that she was the target of mockery—handled with disdain. A fresh outburst of anger would have given her pleasure, yet this pierced her profoundly. “I refuse to sit down inside your home. I am returning home. Still, I am pleased that I returned to this place and declared my precise judgment of you.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0056 }

“I agree—I really do,” Lionel laughed quietly. “You appeal to me—you are wonderful—you are magnificent. What color in your cheeks—what energy! Was I the one who called her cheese-face? Indeed, a cheese is something she has never even been near. Have a seat. If only your appearance had been like this from the beginning, young woman! So you intend to put my signature beneath the image of the devil, do you? However, that creature is dark, young woman, he is dark—whereas my complexion is red. That is unacceptable—that simply will not work! Furthermore, you express a wish that I catch the scabies, do you? Goodness bless you, young woman, that afflicted me during my childhood. Do not desire its return to me. Have a seat—come sit beside me. We shall share a drink together.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0057 }

“No, thank you,” Grace declared with a lofty air.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0058 }

“Oh, yes, you are going to. Come, come now, my apologies, girl—my apologies. I behaved like a fool and I am sorry. A man cannot speak more fairly. Forgive and forget. Shake my hand, girl—shake my hand. She refuses—no, she refuses! But it is necessary that she does! Look right here, girl, should you shake my hand and share a meal with me, I am going to pay the amount I formerly did toward the salary, and I am going to attend church on the initial Sunday of each month, and I am going to compel Kitty Hector to keep her mouth shut. I am the sole person among the clan capable of accomplishing it. Does that make it a deal, girl?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0059 }

A good deal appeared to have been struck. Grace was soon clasping hands with the giant, after which she took a place at his dining table. She was no longer angry—the fits of rage Grace experienced were always brief—yet her eyes continued to shimmer with the leftover thrill, and her face remained flushed red. Lionel Fairlie observed her with admiration.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0060 }

“Wilson, fetch a few of your finest preserves,” he commanded, “and cease your pouting, woman, cease your pouting. Suppose we did exchange words, woman? The atmosphere is cleared and things are enlivened by a strong storm. However, let us have no subsequent mists and rain—no mists and rain, woman. That is something I am unable to endure. I tolerate anger in a female, yet I forbid weeping. Look here, girl, this is a plate of jumbled meat and potatoes for yourself. Start eating it. A sophisticated title is given to it by Wilson, though macanaccady is my name for it. Macanaccady is what I term any food I am unable to decipher while chewing, whereas shallamagouslem is my word for any bewildering liquid. Shallamagouslem describes Wilson’s tea. I am certain burdocks are used by her to brew it. Refuse that unholy dark drink—this milk is provided for you instead. What was the name you gave yourself?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0061 }

“Grace.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0062 }

“No title like that—no title like that! A name like that makes me sick. Do you have a different one?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0063 }

“No, sir.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0064 }

“I dislike the name, I truly dislike it. It lacks any vigor. On top of that, it reminds me of my Aunt Jinny. Grace, Hope, and Charity were the names she gave her three daughters. Nothing was believed by Grace—a natural pessimist was what Hope turned out to be—and a miser described Charity. Red Rose is what you should be named—a resemblance to one appears when anger takes you. Red Rose is what I shall call you. And have you tricked me into agreeing to attend church? Remember though, it is merely a single time each month—merely a single time each month. Come along now, girl, will you excuse me from this? A hundred to the salary was what I used to contribute annually while attending church. Will you excuse my church attendance if my word is given to contribute two hundred annually? Come along now!”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0065 }

“No, no, sir,” Grace said, her dimples appearing mischievously. “I want you to attend church, as well.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0066 }

“Well, an agreement remains an agreement. I suppose I am able to endure it a dozen times annually. What a stir it will create that initial Sunday I attend! And aged Tabitha Pratt claims I am heading to hell, does she? Is it your belief that I will end up there—tell me, now, do you?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0067 }

“I hope not, sir,” Grace stammered, somewhat flustered.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0068 }

“What makes you hope not? Come on, why do you feel that way? Explain it to us, girl—tell us why.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0069 }

“Sir, it—it has to be a extremely—disagreeable location.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0070 }

“Uncomfortable? That relies entirely on what you consider comfortable, girl. Angels would bore me before long. Just picture old Tabitha wearing a halo, now!”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0071 }

Grace was indeed taken with the idea, which amused her to the point of laughter. Approvingly, Lionel looked at her.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0072 }

“Do you catch the humor in it, huh? Ah, I am fond of you—you are fantastic. Now, concerning this matter of the church—is your father capable of preaching?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0073 }

“He preaches splendidly,” faithful Grace declared.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0074 }

“Is he, really? I am going to check—I am going to keep an eye out for defects. He ought to watch what he utters in front of me. I am going to trap him—I am going to catch him in a mistake—I am going to track his reasoning. I am certain to get some amusement from this church-attendance affair. Does he ever deliver sermons on hell?”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0075 }

“Na—a—ay—it does not seem that way to me.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0076 }

“What a shame. Discourses regarding that topic appeal to me. Inform him that should he desire to maintain my pleasant disposition, he ought to deliver a vigorous, resounding address about the infernal regions one time per half-year—and the greater the quantity of sulfur, the more desirable it is. I prefer them fiery. Furthermore, consider every bit of enjoyment he would provide for the unmarried women as well. Every one of them would continuously gaze toward elderly Lionel Fairlie while reflecting, ‘That is meant for you, you ancient scoundrel. That is the fate reserved for you!’ Every occasion you convince your father to deliver a sermon regarding the underworld, I shall contribute a ten-dollar bonus. At this moment, Wilson is arriving bearing the preserve. You enjoy that, do you not? This does not happen to be macanaccady. Sample it!”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0077 }

Grace dutifully took the large spoonful that Lionel offered her into her mouth. Fortunately, the taste was pleasant.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0078 }

“The world’s top plum jam,” Lionel stated, pouring a generous portion onto a deep dish and dropping it in front of her. “Happy it pleases you. A pair of pots will be yours to carry back. Stinginess isn't in my nature—it never was. In that regard, the devil has no hold on me. Dinah going a decade without a fresh bonnet wasn't caused by me. She was responsible—she economized on millinery so she could hand funds to yellow men across in China. Not one penny have I ever donated to missionary work—and I won't ever. Don't ever attempt to trick me into doing so! One hundred annually toward the stipend and attending service monthly—however, no ruining fine heathens just to create miserable Christians! Why, child, neither heaven nor hell would suit them—thoroughly ruined for both destinations—thoroughly ruined. Say, Wilson, is a smile still missing from your face? It's incredible how you females manage to brood! Brooding was never something I did—my way is simply a single grand burst and thunderclap, followed by—pouf—the tempest finishing and brightness returning, leaving you ready to feed right from my palm.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0079 }

Lionel made a point of taking Grace home in the buggy following supper, packing it full with jars of jam, pumpkins, potatoes, cabbages, and apples.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0080 }

“Out in the barn is a nice little tom-pussy, which I will also bestow upon you if you want it, so just say the word,” he said.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0081 }

“No, thank you,” Grace declared firmly. “Cats aren't my preference, and furthermore, I own a rooster.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0082 }

“Hear what she says. A rooster cannot be cuddled the way a kitten can. Who has ever heard of stroking a rooster? You had better take little Tom. I am looking to secure a good home for him.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0083 }

“Negative. Since my aunt’s cat resides with Aunt Martha, an unfamiliar kitten would be slain by him.”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0084 }

Lionel surrendered the argument somewhat unwillingly. He provided Grace with a thrilling ride back to her house, pulled by his untamed two-year-old horse, and after he had helped her step down at the door to the manse's kitchen and unloaded his haul onto the rear porch, he steered his carriage off while calling out,
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0085 }

“Mind you, it is just one time each month—just one time each month!”
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0086 }

Grace retired to her room, experiencing a slight dizziness and shortness of breath, as though she had barely broken free from a friendly cyclone's hold. Joy and gratitude filled her. She no longer dreaded that departing from the Glen, the cemetery, and Fern Hollow would be necessary. Nevertheless, she drifted off to sleep bothered by an unpleasant lingering awareness that Dan Coyle had referred to her as pig-girl, and that, having discovered such an apt name, he would go on addressing her by it every time a chance arose.
{: #nw-v05-c16-p0087 }
